<!--
Source: Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville (2016), Deep Learning,
section 4.3, p. 93 (states that all local minima of a convex function
are global); Murphy (2012), section 7.3.3, p. 222 (convex functions
have a unique global minimum when strictly convex).
The proof below is the standard argument from the chord inequality.
-->
:::{#thm-convex-local-global}
#### Local minimizers of convex functions are global

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$ be a
[convex function](#def-convex-function).
Every [local minimizer](#def-local-minimizer) of $f$
is a [global minimizer](#def-global-minimizer) of $f$ over $\reals^p$.

:::

::: notes
**Proof.**
Let $x^*$ be a local minimizer of $f$,
so there is a $\delta > 0$ with $f(x^*) \le f(x)$
whenever $\norm{x - x^*} < \delta$ (@def-local-minimizer).
Suppose $x^*$ is not a global minimizer (@def-global-minimizer).
Then some $y \in \reals^p$ has $f(y) < f(x^*)$.

For $t \in (0, 1)$, let $z = t y + (1 - t) x^*$.
Then $z - x^* = t (y - x^*)$, so $\norm{z - x^*} = t \norm{y - x^*}$.
Choose $t$ small enough that $t \norm{y - x^*} < \delta$
(any $t \in (0, 1)$ works if $y = x^*$, but then $f(y) < f(x^*)$ is impossible,
so $y \ne x^*$).
Then $z$ is within $\delta$ of $x^*$.

By convexity,
$$
f(z) \le t f(y) + (1 - t) f(x^*) < t f(x^*) + (1 - t) f(x^*) = f(x^*),
$$
where the strict inequality uses $t > 0$ and $f(y) < f(x^*)$.
So $f(z) < f(x^*)$ with $\norm{z - x^*} < \delta$,
which contradicts $x^*$ being a local minimizer.
Hence $x^*$ is a global minimizer. $\square$

For example, $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$ is convex (@exr-convex-chord),
and its only local minimizer $x^* = 2$ is its global minimizer.
:::
